newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel-PLO crisis deepens after Tel Aviv talks fail.
newsitem.headline: Israel-PLO crisis deepens after Tel Aviv talks fail.

text.p: Israel's defence chief and a Palestinian cabinet minister failed in crisis talks to ease tensions heightened by an Israeli troop redeployment plan that the PLO rejected.

"There is a crisis and the crisis is becoming worse and worse," a visibly angry Palestinian Information Minister Yasser Abed Rabbo said late on Monday after meeting Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai at a Tel Aviv hotel.

Hours earlier, at least 10 Palestinians were injured by Israeli soldiers who used clubs and guns to beat back about 100 Arabs trying to stop workers from opening a road for Jewish settlers near the West Bank town of Hebron, witnesses said.

The clash was the first serious outbreak of Israeli-Arab violence since Palestinian President Yasser Arafat spurned an Israeli decision on Friday to hand over another nine percent of the West Bank to Palestine Liberation Organisation rule.

Palestinians wanted 30 percent and a say in determining the scope of this and two other pullbacks from mainly rural areas of the West Bank which Israel-PLO interim peace deals mandate must be completed by mid-1998.

"The agreements should be respected, the settlements and the confiscation of land should be stopped and the further redeployment should be applied in accordance with the agreement and not in accordance with the intentions of the Israeli government," Abed Rabbo said.

In Washington, President Bill Clinton, speaking at a joint news conference with visiting Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, said he regretted the Israeli house-building decision, but warned the Palestinians that it would be a "terrible mistake" to resort to violence over the matter.
Clinton said recent events showed how difficult it was to make progress towards peace in the Middle East and he called on all parties in the region to redouble their efforts.
Tensions in the West Bank and Gaza have been high since Israel decided last month to build 6,500 houses for Jews on a pine-covered hilltop in Arab East Jerusalem.

Before meeting Mordechai, Abed Rabbo warned of a possible repetition of violence that erupted in September after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu opened a new entrance to an archaeology tunnel near Moslem holy sites in East Jerusalem.

But Mordechai said Israel, which contends a U.S. note attached to a January peace deal with the PLO leaves the scope of the pullbacks to Israel's sole discretion, would not abandon its redeployment plan.

"The Palestinian point of view differs from ours. There are decisions which the Israeli government has taken -- they are valid and will be implemented. But we also have to continue talks with the Palestinians," he told reporters.
Despite the crisis, Netanyahu went ahead with a visit to Russia, leaving instructions behind for Mordechai and Foreign Minister David Levy to hold talks with Palestinian officials, Israel Radio said.
An Israeli official said Israel would not proceed with the redeployment so long as the PLO, which currently has sole control of about three percent of the West Bank, rejected it.
"Arafat in the past has used a controlled crisis as an instrument for winning international attention and political gains," said another Israeli official, who declined to be identified.
"But it's a very dangerous game because it can always lead to Palestinian violence that he may not be able to control," he said.
Israeli security sources said the army has a plan to deploy tanks and snipers in the West Bank if clashes such as those that killed 61 Palestinians and 15 Israelis six months ago broke out again.

In a sign of growing Arab anger over Israel's redeployment plan, the entire Palestinian peace negotiating team led by Mahmoud Abbas, better known as Abu Mazen, resigned on Monday, PLO negotiator Saeb Erekat told Reuters. Arafat has yet to accept the resignations, PLO officials said.
